articles.description:
Short answer: to flip a video with FFmpeg, re-encode through hflip or vflip:
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf hflip -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy flipped.mp4

hflip is a left–right mirror. vflip is a top–bottom mirror. The frame size stays the same (here, 720×1280). That is not a rotate: transpose=1 would turn this clip into 1280×720. And despite what autocomplete offers for "ffmpeg flip video without re encoding", a flip is a video filter, so -c:v copy is rejected: Filtering and streamcopy cannot be used together. Audio can still be stream-copied. Below are pixel-exact measurements on a real 8-second clip, a small Python module, and five pytest checks.

The fixture is a real generated example from Voor's Enzo Fernandez Celebration page: a vertical 720×1280 H.264 + AAC clip, 24 fps, 193 f…
articles.title: How to Flip a Video With FFmpeg (hflip and vflip Are Mirrors, Not Rotates, and -c copy Cannot Do Them)

articles.description:
I'm building Cutora, an editor that makes the first cut of a talking-head video. Most of the interesting problems turned out not to be "AI" problems at all. They're timing problems. Here's how the cut is decided, and where it still goes wrong.
Everything starts from a transcript where every word has a start and end time. The cut is planned on words, then rendered on media. If the word times are wrong, every later rule inherits the error, so most of our bugs live here, not in the "smart" parts.
Long pauses get cut, with a short beat left around the words so speech doesn't sound stapled together. Short pauses stay, because they're how people breathe. We don't expose a millisecond threshold; creators pick a pacing and can restore any single cut on the timeline.
The trap: a loudness threshold …
articles.title: Deciding what to cut in a talking-head video: pauses are easy, retakes are not

Say you're building a TypeScript app that transcribes audio, classifies images, or learns from your own data. How much of the machine learning work can stay in TypeScript?
That depends on the job. Calling a model service keeps the app in TypeScript, but the model runs elsewhere. Running an existing model locally brings its inputs, weights, memory use, and device support into your app. Training your own model adds data preparation, gradients, an optimizer, evaluation, and checkpoints.
I wanted to explore the last two paths in TypeScript, so I've been building Affon, a runtime for numerical computing and machine learning.
Affon's decoder language model app defines attention and embeddings, prepares text batches, trains and evaluates a model, saves checkpoints, and generates text. A saved loc…
articles.title: How far can you take machine learning in TypeScript?
